title: Team inbox for support tickets — plan

goal_inbox.takeaway: Support agents work every ticket from one shared inbox instead of a shared mailbox
goal_inbox.key: Email, chat and web-form tickets land in one queue; each has exactly one owner
goal_inbox.body:
**Goal:** replace the shared `support@` mailbox with a **team inbox** inside the product. Every incoming message, whatever the channel, becomes a ticket with one owner, a status and a history.

- **Today:** five agents read the same mailbox. Two people answer the same customer, or nobody does, and there is no way to see what is waiting.
- **After:** a ticket is assigned the moment it arrives, agents see who is working on what, and a lead sees the queue at a glance.

**Why now:** ticket volume doubled after the spring launch (about 400 a week), and the median first reply went from 3 hours to 11. The two seams we need already exist:
1. The **notifications service** already ingests email for order updates, so inbound mail is a new consumer, not a new pipeline.
2. The **activity feed** component already renders a per-object history, so a ticket's timeline is a reuse, not a rewrite.

items.what: Inbound email parsing: the notifications service already reads mail
Per-object history: the activity feed renders order timelines
Assignment rules and a shared queue with ownership

scope_inbox.takeaway: One inbox for email, chat and web forms; no phone, no social channels in v1
scope_inbox.key: Small enough to ship in a month, big enough to retire the shared mailbox
scope_inbox.body:
**In v1** the inbox covers the three channels that carry 95% of today's volume.

| Channel | Share of tickets | In v1 |
|---|---|---|
| Email | 71% | yes |
| Chat widget | 18% | yes |
| Web form | 6% | yes |
| Phone | 3% | no |
| Social | 2% | no |

**Out** for now: anything that needs a new vendor contract (phone, social), customer-facing ticket portals, and AI-drafted replies. Each is a follow-up with its own plan.

in: **Chat widget** conversations after the agent goes offline
out: SLA reporting beyond first reply time

success_inbox.takeaway: First reply under 4 hours, no ticket answered twice, the mailbox retired
success_inbox.key: Measured from the ticket log for two weeks after the switch
success_inbox.body:
**Success** is measured from the ticket event log, not a survey. We compare the two weeks before the switch with the two weeks after.

- **First reply time:** median under 4 hours during business hours.
- **Double answers:** zero tickets with replies from two agents within 10 minutes of each other.
- **Nothing lost:** every message to support@ appears as a ticket within a minute.
- **Mailbox retired:** nobody on the team opens the shared mailbox in week two.

No ticket answered by two agents
Every inbound email becomes a ticket within a minute
Shared mailbox unused in week two

design_inbox.takeaway: Inbound channels write to one ticket store; the inbox UI reads it and assigns on arrival
design_inbox.key: Three adapters, one store, one assignment step; nothing talks to the mailbox directly
design_inbox.body:
**Design:** each channel has a small adapter that turns its message into a `ticket.message` event. The ticket store folds those events into tickets, and the assignment step picks an owner when a ticket opens.

1. **Adapters** (email, chat, form) normalise sender, subject, body and attachments. The email adapter threads replies by the `In-Reply-To` header, then by a ticket id in the subject.
2. **Ticket store** keeps tickets as events: opened, message, assigned, status changed, note added. Replaying them rebuilds a ticket, which is also how the timeline renders.
3. **Assignment** runs on `ticket.opened`: round robin over agents who are online, skipping anyone over their open-ticket limit. A lead can reassign at any time.
4. **Inbox UI** lists tickets by status and owner, with a detail pane that reuses the activity feed.

Replies go out through the existing notifications service, so outbound mail keeps its templates, tracking and bounce handling.

items.title: Adapters
items.detail: one per channel; normalise and thread

risk_inbox.takeaway: The biggest risks are lost mail during the switch and agents ignoring the new tool
risk_inbox.key: Both are contained by running the mailbox and the inbox side by side for a week
risk_inbox.body:
**Risks**, worst first. The switch is the dangerous moment: if forwarding breaks, customers write into a void.

- **Lost mail:** forwarding from support@ fails silently. Mitigated by keeping the mailbox readable for a week and alerting when the inbound rate drops to zero for 30 minutes.
- **Adoption:** agents keep answering from the mailbox out of habit. Mitigated by making the mailbox read-only on day three.
- **Threading:** replies from some mail clients drop the headers and open a new ticket. Mitigated by the subject-line fallback and a merge button.
- **Load:** a spam wave opens thousands of tickets. Mitigated by the existing spam filter and a per-sender rate limit.

components_inbox.takeaway: Four phases over about three weeks; email first because it is 71% of volume
components_inbox.key: Each phase ships behind a flag and can run alongside the mailbox
components_inbox.body:
**Components and phases.** Email goes first because it carries most of the volume and exercises every part of the design. Chat and the web form are adapters on the same store.

1. **Email inbox:** adapter, ticket store, assignment, list and detail views.
2. **Chat and form:** two more adapters; the UI gains channel badges.
3. **Notes and statuses:** internal notes, waiting-on-customer, auto-reopen on reply.
4. **Switch over:** forwarding, the read-only mailbox, alerts, and the first-reply report.

verification_inbox.takeaway: Each phase is proven by a test that sends real mail through staging
verification_inbox.key: No phase ships until its row is green on staging
verification_inbox.body:
**Verification** runs on staging with a real mailbox, not mocks. Each phase adds one end-to-end test and keeps the earlier ones.

- Send an email, a chat transcript and a form submission; each becomes a ticket.
- Reply from three mail clients; each reply lands on the right ticket.
- Take one agent offline; nothing is assigned to them.

Replies from Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail thread correctly
Offline agents get no new tickets
Chat and form submissions open tickets

q1-assignment.takeaway: Q1: how are new tickets assigned?
q1-assignment.key: Decides whether agents pick work or are handed it
q1-assignment.body: Recommendation: **Round robin**. It spreads the load evenly from day one and needs no rules to maintain.

q2-history.key: Decides whether agents need the mailbox for context after the switch
q2-history.body: Recommendation: **import the last 90 days** so recent conversations keep their history. The user chose a clean start instead and keeps the mailbox read-only as an archive.

- **2026-10-01:** Draft v0 written from the support team's notes and a week of mailbox stats.
- **2026-10-02:** The user decided:

switch-over.takeaway: The switch takes one afternoon and can be rolled back by turning forwarding off
switch-over.key: Forward first, watch for a day, then make the mailbox read-only
switch-over.body:
**Switch-over runbook.** The order matters: forwarding goes on before anyone changes how they work, so a failure only costs a day of double reading.

1. Turn on forwarding from support@ to the inbound address.
2. Watch the inbound rate for a day next to the mailbox.
3. Announce the switch in the support channel.
4. Make the mailbox read-only on day three.
5. Turn off the alert's grace period.

**Rollback:** turn forwarding off. The mailbox still has every message, and tickets opened so far stay in the inbox.

| Step | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| Forwarding on | Ops | Monday 14:00 |
| Side-by-side watch | Support lead | Monday to Tuesday |
| Read-only mailbox | Ops | Wednesday |

Announce the switch in the support channel

options.label: The first public reply by an agent (Recommended)
options.description: Notes and auto-replies don't count. The honest number, and the one customers feel.

options.label: Any agent action
options.description: A note, an assignment or a status change stops the clock. Easy to hit, easy to game.

options.label: The auto-acknowledgement
options.description: Every ticket gets an instant reply. Meaningless as a measure.

q3-sla-clock.takeaway: Q3: what stops the first-reply clock?
q3-sla-clock.key: Decides the number the success criteria are measured against
q3-sla-clock.body: The first-reply time in the success criteria needs a definition. Should an internal note count, or an auto-reply? The options differ in how honest the number is and how easy it is to game.

q4-limits.decision: Soft cap of 15, raised by a lead

options.label: Soft cap of 15, raised by a lead (Recommended)
options.description: Round robin skips agents at 15 open tickets; leads can raise it per agent.

options.label: No cap
options.description: Everyone gets an equal share, however many they already hold.

q4-limits.takeaway: Q4: is there a cap on open tickets per agent?
q4-limits.key: Decides when round robin skips someone
q4-limits.body: Recommendation: **a soft cap of 15** that a lead can raise. Without one, a slow day for one agent becomes a backlog only they can clear.

view.chosen: Soft cap of 15, raised by a lead
view.why: keeps one slow day from becoming a private backlog
view.recommended: Soft cap of 15, raised by a lead

success_lead_view.takeaway: A lead sees the whole queue, by owner and by age, without asking anyone
success_lead_view.key: The lead view is the one screen the support lead opens first every morning
success_lead_view.body:
**Lead view.** The support lead's job today is asking people what they are working on. The inbox replaces that with one screen:

- **By owner:** open tickets per agent, with the oldest highlighted.
- **By age:** anything past 4 hours without a public reply.
- **Waiting on customer:** tickets that reopen automatically when the customer replies.

This view needs no new data: it is a query over the same ticket events the inbox already reads.
